title: The Talking Stage: How Long It Lasts and What Comes Next — cv.cm
description: What the talking stage is, how long it usually lasts, signs it is moving forward or stuck, and the exact words for a calm "what are we" talk.
h1: What is the talking stage, and how long should it last?
answer: The talking stage is the early period when two people chat, flirt and get to know each other without calling it dating yet. There is no fixed rule, but it usually lasts a few weeks, not many months. It is healthy when you meet more often and talk more openly over time. If nothing moves after a month or two, ask a clear, kind question about where it is going.

body: The talking stage is the gap between first interest and a clear relationship. You message often, you may have met once or twice, you both know there is some interest, but neither of you has said "we are dating" or "we are together". It is a normal step, not a problem to fix.

Different places have their own names for it. In Chinese it is often called 暧昧期 (or 曖昧 in Taiwan and Japan), in Korean it is 썸, and English speakers say "talking stage" or "talking to someone". The words differ, but the feeling is the same: you like each other, things are warm, and nothing is decided.

Culture shapes what comes next. In much of China, Taiwan, Japan and Korea, the stage often ends with a confession (告白 / 고백), and after a yes you are a couple. In many Western countries people go on several dates first and define the relationship later, sometimes weeks after things became physical. Neither path is better. What matters is that both people slowly learn they want the same thing.

sections.h: How long the talking stage usually lasts
body: No study sets a correct length, and you should be careful with anyone who promises one. A useful way to think about it is in time spent together, not days on the calendar. Research on new friendships by Jeffrey Hall found that closeness grew with the hours people spent together and with everyday talk, and that it takes dozens of hours to move from acquaintance to friend. Chatting a little each night builds less than one long afternoon together.

In practice, most talking stages that turn into dating move forward within a few weeks to two months. Longer is fine when distance, exams or work really limit how often you can meet, as long as things are still moving. A talking stage that has stayed exactly the same for many months is usually not a stage any more. It has become a habit, or a situationship.

sections.h: Signs it is moving forward vs stuck
body: Words like "I really like talking to you" are nice, but actions over time tell you more. Look at the pattern across two or three weeks, not one good or bad day.

body.note: Reply speed alone says very little. People have work, school and different phone habits. Whether they keep the conversation going and make plans says much more.

sections.h: How to move from talking to dating
body: Moving forward is mostly about three things: more time in person, a clear date, then a clear conversation.

ol: Turn chat into plans. Instead of a third hour of messages, write: "I like talking to you. Want to get coffee on Saturday afternoon?"
Make one plan a real date. Something a bit special, like dinner or a walk at night, so it is not just hanging out with friends.
Notice how it feels. Do you both relax, laugh, want to see each other again? Do they make plans too?
Show your interest clearly. Say it in simple words: "I really enjoy spending time with you."
Have the "what are we" talk, or confess, when you have met several times and the signs are good.

body: If you are in a place where confessing is the usual step, see cv.cm's guide on how to confess your feelings. If you are not sure how to invite someone, see the guide on how to ask someone out.

sections.h: How to have the "what are we" talk
body: This talk does not need to be a big event. Do it in person or on a call if you can, at a calm moment, not in the middle of a fight or after drinking. Start with your own feelings, then ask an open question, then listen.

ul: "I really like where this is going. I'm not seeing anyone else, and I'd like us to be exclusive. How do you feel?"
"I've had a great time these last few weeks. I'd like to know where you see this going."
"I'm looking for a relationship, not just chatting. Is that something you want too?"
If you want to keep it light: "So, are we dating? Because I'd like to be."

body: Then let them answer, even if there is a pause. "I'm not sure yet" is a real answer. You can say: "That's okay. Can we talk again in a few weeks?" If the answer is no, thank them and accept it. A clear no is painful, but it frees you.

The Cambridge Dictionary defines a situationship as a romantic relationship between two people who do not yet consider themselves a couple. A talking stage is meant to lead somewhere. A situationship often has the closeness of a relationship, sometimes including sex, but no plan to define it, and one person often wants more than the other. See cv.cm's slang dictionary for what situationship means and how people use the word.

sections.h: Push-pull games and why they backfire
body: Many people are told to play games in this stage: wait hours before replying, act cold after a warm day, or flirt with others to make the person jealous. In Korean this is called 밀당 (push and pull). It can create excitement for a short time, because uncertainty keeps people thinking about you. But it also teaches the other person that you are hard to read, it attracts people who enjoy games, and it pushes away calm, secure people who simply think you are not interested.

A better rule is to be consistent and honest. Reply when you have time, make plans you keep, and say what you want. Gottman's research on couples describes small "bids for connection" (a question, a joke, a shared photo) and found that couples who usually turn toward each other's bids do better over time. Building that habit now is better practice for a real relationship than any game.
If you notice that you feel anxious when they are slow to reply, or that you go cold when things get close, cv.cm's attachment style test can help you see your own pattern.
It is okay to end a talking stage. Consider stepping back if:

ul: You have asked for clarity and they keep avoiding the question.
They cancel plans often and do not offer new ones.
You only hear from them when they are bored or lonely.
They say they do not want a relationship and you do.
You feel worse about yourself most of the time.

body: You can end it kindly in one message: "I've enjoyed talking to you, but I'm looking for something more clear. I'm going to step back. I wish you well." If the person keeps sending low-effort messages after that, see cv.cm's guide to breadcrumbing.

faq.q: Is it okay to talk to more than one person during the talking stage?
faq.a: In many places, yes, until you agree to be exclusive. But be honest if asked, and do not pretend to be exclusive when you are not.

faq.q: Who should start the "what are we" talk?
faq.a: Whoever wants clarity first. There is no rule about gender or who is older. Starting it shows confidence, not weakness.

faq.q: Can the talking stage happen only over text?
faq.a: It can start that way, especially with someone far away, but it rarely becomes a relationship without calls, video or meetings. Suggest one of those within the first few weeks.

faq.q: Why did they go quiet after the talking stage got serious?
faq.a: They may have lost interest, felt overwhelmed, or be avoiding closeness. Send one calm message asking how they are; if there is still silence, take it as an answer.

faq.q: Is 暧昧 (ambiguity) a bad sign?
faq.a: Not by itself. Some ambiguity is normal early on. It becomes a problem when it lasts for months and one person wants more while the other avoids the question.
